This looks like a map of milk. It's closer to a map of a mutation. Most adult humans stop making the enzyme that digests it — the dark countries are where that switch stopped flipping.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Lactase breaks lactose down. Almost every baby makes it; in most mammals, and in most people, production shuts off after weaning. Roughly 65% of humans alive today lack lactase persistence into adulthood.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

2/ Europe has the steepest gradient anywhere on Earth. Persistence runs from about 15–54% in the southeast to 89–96% in the northwest. Greeks come in near 17%, Sardinians near 14%. Ireland and the Netherlands are the darkest patches here.

3/ The order of events is the surprise. Dairying came first. Farmers were milking animals for millennia before the gene spread — the oldest carrier found in ancient DNA lived in central Europe somewhere around 2450–2140 BCE.

4/ So what were they doing with the milk? Fermenting it. Cheese, yoghurt and soured milk lose most of their lactose in the process. These are workarounds invented long before any body solved the problem biologically.

5/ Which explains the bright patch in Central Asia. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan sit high on milk supply with lactase persistence estimated at only about 11–32% — a dairy culture built on kumis, which ferments away nearly all the lactose.

6/ And it happened more than once. At least six separate mutations are linked to lactase persistence: one that dominates Europe, others in East Africa and around Arabia, spreading with cattle and camel herding respectively.

7/ Two cautions. "Supply" means what's available per person, dairy included and butter excluded — not what anyone drinks. And the genetics are unsettled: some researchers read Europe's gradient as drift as much as selection.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
